At 4:17 every morning, the town’s clocks stopped.

Not all of them. The clock in the bakery continued its red digital blinking. The clock above the train station clicked stubbornly forward, though no train had arrived in twelve years. People’s phones remained accurate. Their ovens did not forget the time. The world, in every practical sense, went on.

But the old clocks stopped.

The one in the mayor’s office. The brass carriage clock in the library. The grandfather clock in the abandoned hotel. The small blue clock hanging above the sink in Apartment 3B, where an elderly woman named Mara lived alone with a cat that had no name.

At 4:17, each hand halted.

No one knew why. Some said it began after the flood, when the river climbed the embankment and swallowed the lower streets. Some said it had always happened and people had only recently learned to notice. The priest called it a reminder. The mechanic called it a coincidence. Children called it the Hour of Ghosts.

Mara called it breakfast.

She rose at 4:17 every morning without an alarm. Her bones knew before the clock did. She put water on the stove, sliced an apple, and fed the cat, who appeared each day at the exact moment she set down the bowl.

The cat had arrived during the flood.

Mara found it on the roof of the post office, drenched and furious, its yellow eyes shining through the rain. She had been there too, waiting for the water to fall. She had been young then, though not young enough to climb easily, and the cat had been smaller than a loaf of bread.

When the rescue boat finally came, the cat leapt into her arms.

Afterward, it followed her home.

She gave it no name because names, Mara believed, were promises. Promises were dangerous things. They grew roots. They pulled you back.

Every morning, she poured tea into two cups.

One for herself.

One for the person who had not returned.

The cup remained untouched until the tea went cold. Then she emptied it into the sink and washed both cups.

On the morning the clocks stopped, someone knocked at her door.

Three knocks.

Mara looked at the blue clock above the sink. Its hands were fixed at 4:17.

The cat lifted its head.

Three more knocks.

“Come in,” Mara said.

The door opened.

A boy stood in the hallway, perhaps ten years old, perhaps older. He wore a yellow raincoat though the sky outside was clear. His hair dripped onto the floor. In his hands he held a small wooden box.

Mara knew him.

Not his face, exactly. She knew the shape of his silence.

“You’re late,” she said.

The boy looked down at the box. “I got lost.”

“Everyone does.”

He stepped inside.

The cat circled his legs, sniffed his shoes, and hissed.

“That’s all right,” Mara told it. “He hasn’t earned your trust.”

The boy glanced at the two cups on the table. “Who are you waiting for?”

“No one.”

“Then why are there two?”

Mara sat down. The chair across from her seemed to move slightly, as if someone had just pulled it back.

“Who sent you?”

The boy placed the wooden box on the table. It was old, darkened by water, and carved with tiny waves. Mara recognized it immediately.

Her hands began to tremble.

Inside the box, she knew, was a brass key.

She had watched that key disappear beneath the flood.

The boy pushed the box toward her.

“Open it,” he said.

“I don’t think so.”

“You’ve been waiting thirty years.”

“I have not.”

The boy’s eyes were the pale gray of river stones. “You make tea for him every morning.”

Mara stood so quickly her chair toppled backward.

The cat fled beneath the stove.

Outside, somewhere beyond the apartment walls, a clock began to strike. Once. Twice. Three times. The sound was deep and distant, as though it came from beneath the earth.

Mara reached for the box.

The moment her fingers touched the lid, the apartment filled with the smell of rain.

Not the clean scent of spring rain, but the heavy, muddy breath of the river. Water rushed in her ears. The kitchen vanished.

She was standing in the old house again.

Her husband was at the window, tying a rope around his waist. Their daughter, Lena, was asleep upstairs. The river had already crossed the garden.

“Take her,” Mara said.

“I’m going back for the neighbors.”

“You can’t.”

He kissed her forehead. He smelled of smoke and wet wool.

“I’ll be back before breakfast.”

Then he opened the door.

The water took him.

Mara remembered screaming. She remembered the house breaking apart. She remembered finding Lena on the roof, alive, clutching a blue clock that had been torn from the kitchen wall.

She remembered the rescue boat.

She remembered the long years afterward.

But she did not remember Lena growing up.

She did not remember Lena leaving.

She did not remember Lena dying.

She had stored that memory somewhere unreachable, somewhere beneath the hour that stopped.

The vision loosened.

Mara opened her eyes.

The boy was still there.

“Who are you?” she whispered.

He looked toward the hallway.

A woman stood in the doorway.

She was tall and thin, with wet hair and a blue clock tucked beneath one arm. She wore a red sweater Mara had knitted when Lena was sixteen. Her face was older than Mara remembered and younger than Mara felt.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

Then Mara said, “You’re late.”

The woman smiled.

“I got lost.”

Mara crossed the room.

She did not ask where her daughter had been. She did not ask why she had come as a woman, or why the boy wore a yellow raincoat, or whether there was truly a river somewhere beyond the walls.

She simply held out her arms.

Lena stepped into them.

The blue clock slipped to the floor.

Its hands moved.

4:18.

Across town, every old clock began ticking again.

The bakery clock. The station clock. The mayor’s clock. The grandfather clock in the abandoned hotel.

And in Apartment 3B, Mara poured the tea into two cups.

This time, neither one went cold.
